HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) must get your tax return and any money you owe by the deadline.

If you do not know your profit for the whole tax year, you still need to send a tax return. Check how to send a return if you do not know your profit for the whole year.

The last tax year started on 6 April 2025 and ended on 5 April 2026. The deadline for earlier tax returns has passed and you may have to pay a penalty. Send your tax return or payment as soon as possible to avoid further penalties.

## Telling HMRC you need to complete a return

You must tell HMRC by 5 October if you need to do a tax return for last year and one of these is true:

- you have never sent a tax return before
- you registered before but did not need to send a tax return for the tax year 2024 to 2025

You can tell HMRC by registering for Self Assessment. Check how to register for Self Assessment.

### If you register after 5 October 2026

HMRC will send you a letter or email. It will tell you a different date to send your tax return by. This new date will be 3 months from the date on the letter or email.

You must still pay the tax you owe by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027. If you do not, you will get a penalty.

## Sending a paper tax return

HMRC must get your paper tax return by 11:59pm on 31 October 2026. If they do not get it by then, you get a late filing penalty.

You can send it from 6 April 2026. You must make sure HMRC gets it by 31 October 2026.

## Submitting an online tax return

You must send your online tax return by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027. If you do not, you will get a late filing penalty.

If you want to pay your Self Assessment bill through your tax code, you must submit it by 11:59pm on 30 December 2026. If you miss this deadline, you must pay another way.

You can submit your return any time from 6 April 2026 up to the deadline.

### Paying the tax you owe

You must pay your Self Assessment tax by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027. You will get a penalty if you do not.

There is a second deadline on 31 July. This is for 'payments on account' if you pay towards your bill.

You can work out your Self Assessment tax bill before you send your tax return:

- to give you an idea of your likely bill
- to let you budget and pay on time

Find help to understand the tax you owe.

### Trustees of a registered pension scheme or non-resident companies

HMRC must get a paper tax return by 31 January 2027. You cannot send the return online.

You can send it from 6 April 2026. You must send it on or after this date.

### Partnership returns if you have a company as a partner

If your partnership has an accounting date between 1 February and 5 April, and one partner is a limited company:

- The deadline for online returns is 12 months from the accounting date
- The deadline for paper returns is 9 months from the accounting date

You will get a penalty if you need to do a tax return and:

- you send your return late
- you pay your tax bill late

You can guess your penalty for late Self Assessment tax returns and payments.

### If you register for Self Assessment late

If you register after 5 October and do not pay all your tax bill by 31 January, you may get a ‘failure to notify’ penalty.

This penalty depends on the amount still left to pay. You will get it within 12 months after HMRC gets your Self Assessment tax return.

You can find more information on ‘failure to notify’ penalties.

### If you send your tax return late

You will get these late filing penalties:

- an initial £100 penalty
- after 3 months, daily penalties of £10 per day. The total is up to a maximum of £900
- after 6 months, a penalty of 5% of the tax due or £300. You pay whichever is greater
- after 12 months, another 5% or £300 charge. You pay whichever is greater

To avoid this, send your Self Assessment tax return as soon as possible.

All partners will get a penalty if a partnership tax return is late.

### If you pay your tax late

You will get a penalty. The penalty is 5% of the tax you did not pay. You will get this penalty at these times:

- 30 days
- 6 months
- 12 months

You will also pay interest on the amount you owe. To avoid this, pay your Self Assessment tax bill as soon as possible.

Find out what happens if you do not pay your tax bill.

### Check your State Pension

Your State Pension amount depends on your National Insurance record.

Check your State Pension forecast to see how much you could get when you reach State Pension age. It also shows your National Insurance record.

The full rate of the new State Pension is £241.30 a week. Your amount could be different depending on:

- if you were contracted out before 2016
- the number of National Insurance qualifying years you have
- if you paid into the Additional State Pension before 2016

Find out what tax you might pay on your retirement income. This includes if you retire abroad.

## If you’re getting less than £241.30 a week

You might need more years of National Insurance. This will raise your State Pension.

### If your National Insurance record started before April 2016

You may have been contracted out.

*   When you were contracted out, you or your employer paid more into your workplace or private pension.
*   When you were contracted out, you or your employer paid less into your State Pension.

If you were contracted out, you usually need more than 35 qualifying years for the full rate of new State Pension.

### If your National Insurance record started after April 2016

If your National Insurance record started after April 2016, you need 35 qualifying years for the full rate of new State Pension.

## If you're getting more than £241.30 a week

You paid into the Additional State Pension before 2016. Under the old rules, you would have got more State Pension. You will get a 'protected payment'. This is paid on top of the full rate of new State Pension.

### Annual increases

Your new State Pension goes up every year. It goes up by the biggest of these three amounts:

- earnings – how much wages went up in Great Britain on average
- prices – how much prices went up in the UK (measured by the Consumer Prices Index, or CPI)
- 2.5%

If you have a protected payment, your pension goes up every year with the CPI.

### How much you get

There are 2 Child Benefit rates.

| Who the allowance is for | Rate (weekly) |
| --- | --- |
| Eldest or only child | £27.05 |
| Additional children | £17.90 per child |

You must contact the Child Benefit Office if you get too much money. You must also contact them if you get too little money.

Your Child Benefit counts towards the benefit cap. If the cap affects you, you will still get the full Child Benefit amount. But your other benefits might be reduced.

### If families split up

If a family splits up, you get £27.05 a week for the eldest child.

If you have 2 children:
* one lives with you
* one lives with someone else (for example, your ex-partner)

You will each get £27.05 a week.

If you both claim for the same child, only one of you will get Child Benefit for them.

If you’re entitled to Child Benefit for any other children, you’ll get £17.90 for each child.

### If families join together

If you move in with a partner who also claims Child Benefit, you get £27.05 for the eldest child in the household. You get £17.90 for any younger children.

You and your partner can claim for different children. But if you live together, you cannot both claim at the higher rate. You may have to pay back some money if you do.

You must report the change to your family circumstances.

### If you or your partner earn over the threshold

If you or your partner earns more than the limit, you might have to pay the High Income Child Benefit Charge.

Your adjusted net income is your total taxable income. It is your total before personal allowances and after things like Gift Aid. Your total taxable income includes interest from savings and dividends.

If you have to pay the charge, you can still get the other benefits of Child Benefit. This includes National Insurance credits. The charge will not cost more than the amount you get from Child Benefit payments.

Use the Child Benefit tax calculator to see if your adjusted net income is over the limit. If it is, the calculator will tell you how much charge you must pay.

If you and your partner both earn more than the limit, the person with the higher adjusted net income must pay the charge.

If you or your partner earns £20,000 or more above the limit (£10,000 or more before April 2024), you will pay an amount equal to your Child Benefit payments. You will get no extra money from Child Benefit.

You can make a claim and choose not to get payments if you do not want to pay the charge. You can still get the other benefits from Child Benefit. This includes National Insurance credits.

### If you’re under 16

You can claim for your own child.
Or, someone responsible for you can claim for your child for you.
You will usually get more if you claim yourself.

Universal Credit pays you once a month. The amount you get depends on:

- your standard allowance
- any extra amounts you get
- any money taken off your payment
- if you’re working, how much you earn

Use a benefits calculator to see how much you could get.

If you get Universal Credit, you earn Class 3 National Insurance credits. These count towards your State Pension.

### Standard allowance

You get one standard allowance for your home.

| How much you get | Monthly standard allowance |
|---|---|
| If you are single and under 25 | £338.58 |
| If you are single and 25 or over | £424.90 |
| If you live with your partner and you are both under 25 | £528.34 (for you both) |
| If you live with your partner and either of you are 25 or over | £666.97 (for you both) |

## Extra amounts

You may get more money than your standard allowance if you are eligible.

You must report changes when you become eligible for an extra amount. These are not added automatically. For example, if you become a carer, you need to tell DWP. The carer's element of Universal Credit is not added automatically if you start getting Carer's Allowance.

### If you have children

You get £303.94 a month for each child that lives with you.

If your first child was born before 6 April 2017, you get an extra £47.94 a month for that child.

You get money for each child until 31 August after their:

- 16th birthday

- 19th birthday, if they are in eligible education or training – for example, they are studying for GCSEs, A levels, BTECs, Scottish Highers and SVQs or NVQs up to level 3

### If your child has a disability

You might get an extra monthly amount if any of your children are disabled.

You get either:

- £164.79 - the lower amount

- £514.71 - the higher amount

The higher amount is for a child who:

- gets the highest rate of the care component of Disability Living Allowance (DLA) for children

- gets the higher rate of the daily living part of Personal Independence Payment (PIP)

- is blind or severely sight impaired

The lower amount is for a child who gets any other rate of either DLA for children, or PIP.

### Childcare costs

You can claim back up to 85% of your childcare costs if you are working. If you live with your partner, both of you need to be working. One of you does not need to work if they cannot work due to a disability or health condition.

The childcare must be from a registered provider. You can get help paying for childcare including nurseries, childminders, breakfast clubs, after school care and holiday clubs.

The most you can get each month is:

- £1,071.09 for one child

- £1,836.16 for 2 or more children

You must pay your childcare costs up front. You claim the money back as part of your payment. You can get support to help you pay your childcare costs up front. Talk to your work coach after you have made your claim.

Read more about childcare costs and Universal Credit.

### If you have a disability or health condition

You might get an extra monthly amount if you cannot work because of a health condition, disability or long-term illness.

| How much you'll get | Extra monthly amount |

| If you have a severe health condition or disability that is unlikely to change or you are nearing the end of your life | £429.80 |

| If your health condition or disability is assessed as less severe or your condition may improve over time | £217.26 |

There are different rules if you reported a health condition before 6 April 2026.

If you live with your partner and you both have limited capability for work and work-related activity, you get only one extra monthly amount. You get the higher amount if one of you is eligible for it.

If you get the severe disability premium and you are moving to Universal Credit, you might also get a 'transitional protection' payment.

Read more about health conditions, disability and Universal Credit.

### If you care for someone who gets a health or disability-related benefit

You could get an extra amount called a 'carer's element'. This is added to your Universal Credit if you care for someone who gets one of these benefits:

- Adult Disability Payment – standard or enhanced award

- Armed Forces Independence Payment

- Attendance Allowance

- Child Disability Payment – middle or highest care award

- Constant Attendance Allowance - full day rate, intermediate rate or exceptional rate with Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit

- Constant Attendance Allowance - full day rate with a War Disablement Pension

- Disability Living Allowance – middle or highest care rate

- Personal Independence Payment – either rate of the daily living part

You must provide care for them for at least 35 hours a week.

You get an extra monthly amount of £209.34. If you live with your partner and you both care for the same person, you get only one extra monthly amount.

You may also be eligible for Carer's Allowance.

This is on top of any extra amount you get if you have a disabled child.

If you are getting an extra amount because you have limited capability for work and work related activity (LCWRA), you cannot get the carer's element.

If the person you care for gets the severe disability premium, it stops when you claim the carer's element of Universal Credit.

### Housing costs

You could get money to help pay your housing costs. The payment can cover rent and some service charges.

If you are a homeowner, you might be able to get a loan to help with interest payments on your mortgage.

## Money taken from your payment

Your payment may be less if any of these are true:

- you are paying back a Universal Credit advance

- you would get more than the benefit cap allows

- you were paid too much benefit before

- you owe money for Council Tax, court fines, electricity, gas, water or Child Maintenance

- you pay your gas or electricity bill from your Universal Credit payment

- you have a paid job

- you have other income, such as from pensions or some other benefits

- you have more than £6,000 in money, savings and investments

If you have more than £6,000 in money, savings and investments, your payment goes down by £4.35 for every £250 you have between £6,000 and £16,000. Another £4.35 is taken if there is any money left over that is not a full £250.

Learn more about money taken from your Universal Credit payment.

### Benefits that change how much Universal Credit you get

You can get Universal Credit with other benefits. Your Universal Credit payment goes down by the amount of the other benefit. This happens if you get Universal Credit and any of these benefits:

- Armed Forces Pensions

- Carer’s Allowance

- Carer Support Payment (Scotland)

- Incapacity Benefit

- Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit (not including any extra money for constant attendance or exceptionally severe disablement)

- Maternity Allowance

- Severe Disablement Allowance

- State Pension

- Widowed Mother’s Allowance

- Widowed Parent’s Allowance

- New Style Employment and Support Allowance (ESA)

- New Style Jobseeker’s Allowance (JSA)

### Claiming Universal Credit and New Style ESA or JSA

You might get Universal Credit with New Style ESA or JSA.

If you do, your Universal Credit payment is less. It is less by the amount of New Style ESA or JSA you get.

New Style ESA and JSA are paid more often than Universal Credit.

You also get different National Insurance credits. These count towards your State Pension. They can help you get other benefits.

You might keep getting New Style ESA or JSA if your situation changes. This can happen if your Universal Credit payment is less or stops. For example:

- your partner's income increases
- you have more than £16,000 in savings

Check if you can get:

- New Style Jobseeker's Allowance
- New Style Employment and Support Allowance

### Moving to Universal Credit from other benefits

If you apply for Universal Credit, you keep getting your current benefit for 2 more weeks. You must still be eligible for your current benefit.

This only applies if you are getting income-related Employment and Support Allowance or Housing Benefit.

You do not need to pay back the extra payments. These payments will not affect the Universal Credit you might get.

If you get a Migration Notice letter telling you to claim Universal Credit, you might also get a ‘transitional protection’ payment.

### If your Universal Credit claim is reviewed

Your claim might be checked. This is to make sure you get the right money and support. Find out more about Universal Credit reviews.

### You may get Carer’s Allowance if:
- You meet certain rules.
- The person you care for meets certain rules.
- The care you give meets certain rules.

## The person you care for

The person you care for must already get one of these benefits:

- Personal Independence Payment - daily living component

- Disability Living Allowance - the middle or highest care rate

- Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance - the middle or highest care rate

- Attendance Allowance

- Pension Age Disability Payment

- Constant Attendance Allowance at or above the normal maximum rate with an Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit

- Constant Attendance Allowance at the basic (full day) rate with a War Disablement Pension

- Armed Forces Independence Payment

- Child Disability Payment - the middle or highest care rate

- Adult Disability Payment - daily living component at the standard or enhanced rate

### If you care for the person with others

You cannot get Carer’s Allowance if you share the care of someone and the other carer is already claiming:

- Carer’s Allowance for that person

- Carer Support Payment for that person

- the extra amount of Universal Credit for caring for someone who gets a disability-related benefit for that person

If you want to get Carer’s Allowance, speak to the other carer about changing their benefits.

If the other carer does not want to do that, you can still apply for Carer’s Allowance. The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) will decide who should receive the benefit.

## The type of care you provide

You must care for at least 35 hours a week.
This care can be:
- helping with washing and cooking
- taking the person to a doctor’s appointment
- helping with household tasks, like managing bills and shopping

## Your eligibility

You must meet all of these conditions:

- you are 16 or older
- you care for someone for at least 35 hours each week
- you have lived in England, Scotland, or Wales for at least 2 of the last 3 years (this rule does not apply if you are a refugee or have humanitarian protection status)
- you normally live in England or Wales, or you live abroad as a member of the armed forces (you might still qualify if you move to or already live in an EEA country or Switzerland)
- you are not in full-time education
- you are not studying for 21 hours a week or more
- you are not under immigration control
- your earnings are £204 or less each week after tax, National Insurance, and expenses

If you live in Scotland, you must apply for Carer Support Payment instead of Carer's Allowance.

If you are from the EU, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, or Liechtenstein, you and your family usually need settled or pre-settled status under the EU Settlement Scheme to get Carer's Allowance. The deadline to apply to the scheme was 30 June 2021 for most people, but you might still be able to apply. Check if you can still apply to the EU Settlement Scheme.

### Calculating your earnings

Your earnings are any income from working or being self-employed after tax, National Insurance, and expenses.

Expenses can include:

- 50% of your pension contributions
- equipment you need for your job, for example specialist clothing
- travel costs between different workplaces that your employer does not pay for, for example fuel or train fares
- business costs if you are self-employed, for example a computer you only use for work

If you pay a carer to look after the disabled person or your children while you work, you can count care costs that are less than or equal to 50% of your earnings as an expense. The carer must not be your spouse, partner, parent, child, or sibling.

Example

You earn £100 a week (after tax, National Insurance, and other expenses) and spend £60 a week on care while you work. You can count £50 of this as an expense.

Payments that do not count as earnings include:

- money you get from an occupational or private pension
- contributions towards your living or accommodation costs from someone you live with (they cannot be a tenant or boarder)
- the first £20 a week and 50% of any extra income you get from someone boarding in your home
- a loan or advance payment from your employer

### If you get State Pension

You cannot get the full amount of both Carer’s Allowance and your State Pension at the same time.

If your pension is £86.45 a week or more, you will not get a Carer’s Allowance payment.

If your pension is less than £86.45 a week, you’ll get a Carer’s Allowance payment to make up the difference.

### If you get Pension Credit

If your State Pension is more than £86.45 a week, you will not get a Carer's Allowance payment.

But your Pension Credit payments will go up instead.

### Pension Credit tops up:

- Your weekly income to £238 if you are single
- Your joint weekly income to £363.25 if you have a partner

You may get more money if you have other duties and costs.

The top up and the extra money are called 'Guarantee Credit'.

### If you have a severe disability

You could get an extra £86.05 a week if you get any of these:

- Attendance Allowance
- the middle or highest rate of the care component of Disability Living Allowance (DLA)
- the daily living component of Personal Independence Payment (PIP)
- Armed Forces Independence Payment
- the daily living component of Adult Disability Payment
- Pension Age Disability Payment
- the middle or highest rate of the care component of Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance

### If you care for another adult

You could get an extra £48.15 a week if:

- you get Carer’s Allowance

- you get Carer Support Payment

- you have claimed Carer’s Allowance but do not get paid because you already get another benefit paying a higher amount

If you and your partner both claim or get Carer’s Allowance, you can both get this extra amount.

## If you’re responsible for children or young people

You can get extra money for each child or young person you look after who lives with you.

You get £69.98 a week for each child or young person.
This goes up to £81.07 a week for the first child if they were born before 6 April 2017.

You get this extra money until 31 August after they turn:

- 16

- 19, if they are in eligible education or training. This includes studying for GCSEs, A levels, BTECs, Scottish Highers, and SVQs or NVQs up to level 3

If they are in education, it must be for more than 12 hours a week on average.

### If the child or young person is disabled

If the child or young person is disabled, you could get extra money too.

You could get an extra £37.93 a week if the child or young person gets:

- Disability Living Allowance (DLA) for children - lowest or middle rate of the care component or any rate of the mobility component
- Child Disability Payment - lowest or middle rate of the care component or any rate of the mobility component
- Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance - lowest or middle rate of the care component or any rate of the mobility component
- Personal Independence Payment (PIP) - standard rate of the daily living component or any rate of the mobility component
- Adult Disability Payment - standard rate of the daily living component or any rate of the mobility component

You could get an extra £118.46 a week if the child or young person gets:

- Disability Living Allowance (DLA) for children - highest rate of the care component
- Child Disability Payment - highest rate of the care component
- Scottish Adult Disability Living Allowance - highest rate of the care component
- Personal Independence Payment (PIP) - enhanced rate of the daily living component
- Adult Disability Payment - enhanced rate of the daily living component

You might also get money if they are blind or severely sight impaired.

### If you have housing costs

You can get extra money to cover housing costs. This can cover:

- ground rent if your property is a leasehold
- some service charges
- charges for tents and site rents

The extra money you get depends on your housing costs.

If you get Pension Credit, you may also get:

- Council Tax Reduction
- Housing Benefit if you rent the property you live in
- Support for Mortgage Interest if you own the property you live in

### If you have savings or a second pension

You might get the 'Savings Credit' part of Pension Credit if both of these are true:

- you reached State Pension age before 6 April 2016
- you saved some money for retirement, for example a personal or workplace pension

If you are single, you can get up to £17.96 Savings Credit a week. If you have a partner, you can get up to £20.10 a week.

You might still get some Savings Credit even if you do not get the Guarantee Credit part of Pension Credit.

## Other help if you get Pension Credit

If you get Pension Credit, you will get cold weather payments automatically.

You can also do these things if the conditions match:

- apply for a free TV licence if you are 75 or over
- get help with NHS costs if you get the Guarantee Credit part of Pension Credit

NHS costs can include things like prescriptions, dental treatment, glasses and transport costs for hospital appointments.

### Get help with extra amounts

Call the Pension Service helpline if you are not sure if you can get extra amounts.

Pension Service helpline

Telephone: 0800 99 1234

Relay UK (if you cannot hear or speak on the phone): 18001 then 0800 99 1234

British Sign Language (BSL) video relay service if you are on a computer - find out how to use the service on mobile or tablet

Monday to Friday, 8am to 6pm (except public holidays)

Find out about call charges

### Statutory Maternity Pay (SMP)

You get SMP for up to 39 weeks.

Here is what you get:

- For the first 6 weeks, you get 90% of your average weekly earnings (before tax). This is what you get for 6 weeks.
- For the next 33 weeks, you get £194.32 or 90% of your average weekly earnings. You get whichever amount is lower. This is what you get for 33 weeks.

SMP is paid like your wages. It is paid monthly or weekly. Tax and National Insurance are taken from your pay.

Use the maternity planner to work out how much pay you could get.

If you take Shared Parental Leave, you get Statutory Shared Parental Pay (ShPP). You get ShPP of £194.32 a week or 90% of your average weekly earnings. You get whichever amount is lower.

### Start date

SMP usually starts when you take your maternity leave.

SMP starts automatically if you are off work because you are ill with a pregnancy problem. This is if you are off in the 4 weeks before the week your baby is due. The week runs from Sunday to Saturday.

### Problems and disputes

Ask your employer to explain your SMP if you think it is not right.

If you disagree about the amount, contact the Statutory Payment Disputes Team.

If your employer cannot pay (for example because they are insolvent), contact the Statutory Payment Disputes Team.

### Statutory Sick Pay (SSP)

- If you qualify, you get **£123.25 a week** or **80%** of your normal weekly earnings – whichever is lower.
- You get this pay for up to **28 weeks**.
- You get paid for every full day you are sick and would have worked.
- Your employer uses your average weekly earnings from an **8-week period** to work out your pay.
- You still qualify if you started your job recently and have not yet received **8 weeks'** pay.
- Ask your employer to find out more.

### How you're paid

Your boss pays SSP like your normal pay. They pay it weekly or monthly.

If you have more than one job, each boss may pay you SSP.

Tax and National Insurance will be taken out.

If you think you did not get the right amount of SSP, talk to your boss. If you are still not happy, call the HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) enquiry line.

### Your wage depends on your age and if you are an apprentice.

This page is also in Welsh (Cymraeg).

You must be at least:

- school leaving age to get the National Minimum Wage
- aged 21 to get the National Living Wage - the minimum wage will still apply for workers aged 20 and under

## Current rates

The rates change on 1 April every year.

| | 21 and over | 18 to 20 | Under 18 | Apprentice |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| April 2026 | £12.71 | £10.85 | £8 | £8 |
| April 2027 | £13.21 | £11.27 | £8.31 | £8.31 |

### Apprentices

You get the apprentice rate if you are either:

- aged under 19

- aged 19 or over and in the first year of your apprenticeship

Example

An apprentice aged 21 in the first year of their apprenticeship gets £8 an hour.

You get the minimum wage for your age if you both:

- are aged 19 or over

- have completed the first year of your apprenticeship

Example

An apprentice aged 21 who has completed the first year of their apprenticeship gets £12.71 an hour.

## Previous rates

These rates were for the National Living Wage and the National Minimum Wage from April 2019.

### Rates between 1 April 2024 and 31 March 2026

Since 1 April 2024, the National Living Wage is for people aged 21 and over.

| | 21 and over | 18 to 20 | Under 18 | Apprentice |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| April 2025 to March 2026 | £12.21 | £10 | £7.55 | £7.55 |
| April 2024 to March 2025 | £11.44 | £8.60 | £6.40 | £6.40 |

### Rates between 1 April 2021 and 31 March 2024

Between 1 April 2021 and 31 March 2024, the National Living Wage was for people aged 23 and over.

| | 23 and over | 21 to 22 | 18 to 20 | Under 18 | Apprentice |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| April 2023 to March 2024 | £10.42 | £10.18 | £7.49 | £5.28 | £5.28 |
| April 2022 to March 2023 | £9.50 | £9.18 | £6.83 | £4.81 | £4.81 |
| April 2021 to March 2022 | £8.91 | £8.36 | £6.56 | £4.62 | £4.30 |

### Rates before 1 April 2021

Before 1 April 2021, the National Living Wage was for people aged 25 and over.

| | 25 and over | 21 to 24 | 18 to 20 | Under 18 | Apprentice |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| April 2020 to March 2021 | £8.72 | £8.20 | £6.45 | £4.55 | £4.15 |
| April 2019 to March 2020 | £8.21 | £7.70 | £6.15 | £4.35 | £3.90 |

## Who gets the minimum wage

Read this to see who gets the minimum wage.

You can use the minimum wage calculator to check if you are being paid the National Minimum Wage or the National Living Wage.

Contact Acas if you are not getting the National Minimum Wage and think you should be.

### When you get the payment

You will get a letter in October or November. It will tell you how much Winter Fuel Payment you get. This is if you are eligible.

If you do not get a letter but think you are eligible, check if you need to make a claim.

### How much you get

The amount you get is based on two things:
*   When you were born
*   Your circumstances between 21 and 27 September 2026

This time is called the 'qualifying week'.

### What is Marriage Allowance?

Marriage Allowance lets you give £1,260 of your Personal Allowance to your husband, wife or civil partner. Your Personal Allowance is the amount you can earn before you pay tax.

This can cut their tax by up to £252 in a tax year (6 April to 5 April the next year).

This guide is also in Welsh (Cymraeg).

### When can you use it?

To use this with your partner, you (the lower earner) must usually have an income below your Personal Allowance. This is usually £12,570.

### How to calculate your savings

You can work out how much tax you can save as a couple.

Call the Income Tax helpline if:
- you get other income like dividends, savings or job benefits
- you do not know your taxable income

If you give some of your Personal Allowance to your partner, you might pay more tax yourself. But you could still pay less tax as a couple.

### Example

Your income is £11,500 and your Personal Allowance is £12,570, so you do not pay tax.

Your partner’s income is £20,000 and their Personal Allowance is £12,570, so they pay tax on £7,430 (their ‘taxable income’). This means as a couple you are paying Income Tax on £7,430.

When you claim Marriage Allowance you give £1,260 of your Personal Allowance to your partner. Your Personal Allowance becomes £11,310. Your partner gets a reduction of £1,260 on their taxable income.

This means you will now pay tax on £190. But your partner will only pay tax on £6,170. As a couple you save money. You only pay Income Tax on £6,360 instead of £7,430. This saves you £214 in tax.

### Who can apply

You can use Marriage Allowance if all of these rules apply:

- You are married or in a civil partnership.
- You do not pay Income Tax. Or your income is below your Personal Allowance (usually £12,570).
- Your partner pays Income Tax at the basic rate. This usually means their income is between £12,571 and £50,270 before they get Marriage Allowance.

You cannot claim Marriage Allowance if you live together but are not married or in a civil partnership.

If you live in Scotland, your partner must pay the starter, basic or intermediate rate. This usually means their income is between £12,571 and £43,662.

Your application for Marriage Allowance will not change if you or your partner:

- Are currently receiving a pension.
- Live abroad. This is okay as long as you get a Personal Allowance.

If you or your partner were born before 6 April 1935, you might get more benefit as a couple. You could apply for Married Couple’s Allowance instead.

You cannot get Marriage Allowance and Married Couple’s Allowance at the same time.

### Backdating your claim

You can backdate your claim to 6 April 2022 (the 2022 to 2023 tax year). This is for any years you were eligible for Marriage Allowance.

Your partner’s tax bill will be reduced. This depends on the Personal Allowance rate for the years you are backdating.

If your partner has died since 5 April 2022 you can still claim. Call the Income Tax helpline. If your partner was the lower earner, the person who manages their tax affairs needs to call.

### Stopping Marriage Allowance

Your Personal Allowance will move to your partner every year. This happens until you cancel Marriage Allowance.

You should cancel if:
- your income changes
- your relationship ends

## If you pay basic rate Income Tax

If you pay basic rate Income Tax, the rate you pay on gains from 6 April 2026 depends on your gain size and your taxable income.

You can see the rates and allowance for previous years.

To work out your rate:

- Work out your taxable income. This is your income minus your Personal Allowance and any other Income Tax reliefs you get.
- Work out your total taxable gains.
- Take your tax-free allowance from your total taxable gains.
- Add this amount to your taxable income.
- If this amount is inside the basic Income Tax band, you pay 18% on gains made from 6 April 2026.
- For any amount over the basic Income Tax band, you pay 24% on gains made from 6 April 2026.

### Example 1

You make a gain on or after 6 April 2026. Your taxable income (your income minus your Personal Allowance and any Income Tax reliefs) is £20,000 and your taxable gains are £12,600.

First, take the Capital Gains tax-free allowance from your taxable gain. For the 2026 to 2027 tax year the allowance is £3,000. This leaves £9,600 to pay tax on.

Add this to your taxable income. Because the total of £29,600 is less than £37,700 (the basic rate band for the 2026 to 2027 tax year), you pay Capital Gains Tax at 18%.

This means you pay £1,728 in Capital Gains Tax.

### Example 2

You make a gain on or after 6 April 2026. Your taxable income (your income minus your Personal Allowance and any Income Tax reliefs) is £20,000 and your taxable gains are £52,600.

First, take the Capital Gains tax-free allowance from your taxable gain. For the 2026 to 2027 tax year the allowance is £3,000. This leaves £49,600 to pay tax on.

Add this to your taxable income. Because the total of £69,600 is more than £37,700 (the basic rate band for the 2026 to 2027 tax year), you pay Capital Gains Tax at 18% on £17,700 and then 24% on £31,900.

This means you pay £10,842.

Inheritance Tax is a tax on what a person leaves behind when they die. This includes their property, money and things they own.

You usually do not need to pay Inheritance Tax if:

- your estate is worth less than £325,000
- you leave everything above £325,000 to your spouse, civil partner, a charity or a community amateur sports club

You might still need to tell the value of the estate even if it is below the threshold.

Your threshold can go up to £500,000 if you give your home to your children, adopted children, foster children, stepchildren or grandchildren.

If you are married or in a civil partnership and your estate is worth less than your threshold, your partner can use any part of your threshold that you did not use when you die.

This guide is also available in Welsh (Cymraeg).

## Inheritance Tax rates

The standard Inheritance Tax rate is 40%. This tax is only on the part of your estate over the threshold.

### Example

Your estate is worth £500,000. Your tax-free threshold is £325,000. The Inheritance Tax charged is 40% of £175,000 (£500,000 minus £325,000).

The estate can pay Inheritance Tax at a reduced rate of 36% on some assets. This happens if you leave 10% or more of the 'net value' to charity in your will. The net value is the estate's total value minus any debts.

### Reliefs and exemptions

Some gifts you give while you are alive may be taxed after your death. 'Taper relief' might mean the Inheritance Tax charged on the gift is less than 40%. This depends on when you gave the gift.

Other reliefs, such as Business Relief or Agricultural Relief, allow some assets to be passed on free of Inheritance Tax or with a reduced bill.

### Who pays the tax to HMRC

Your estate pays the Inheritance Tax to HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC). The person who handles your estate pays this. This person is called the ‘executor’ if you have a will.

Your beneficiaries (the people who inherit your estate) do not usually pay tax on what they get. They may have other taxes to pay. For example, they might pay tax if they get rental income from a house you left them in your will.

People you give gifts to might have to pay Inheritance Tax. This is only if you give away more than £325,000 and die within 7 years.

- **Copayment**: This is a set amount you pay for a service every time you get it.

You should sign up for Medicare during your Initial Enrollment Period. Do this unless you have other health coverage that works like Medicare. This other coverage might come from an employer. If you do not sign up, you may have to pay extra. This extra cost is called a late enrollment penalty.

Late enrollment penalties:

- Are added to your monthly premium.
- Are not a one-time late fee.
- Are usually charged for as long as you have that type of coverage. For most people, this penalty lasts for a lifetime. The Part A penalty is different.
- Go up the longer you wait to sign up. They are based on how long you go without coverage like Medicare. Find out when you should sign up to avoid penalties.

## Part A late enrollment penalty

- Some people must buy Part A because they do not qualify for premium-free Part A.
Do I qualify for premium-free Part A?
- If you must buy Part A, and you do not buy it when you are first eligible for Medicare, your monthly premium may go up 10%.
- You must pay the penalty for twice the number of years you did not sign up.

Example:
If you were eligible for Part A for 2 years but did not sign up, you must pay the higher premium for 4 years. You usually do not have to pay a penalty if you meet certain conditions that let you sign up for Part A during a Special Enrollment Period. Find out if you are eligible for a Special Enrollment Period.

## Part B late enrollment penalty

- You will not pay a Part B penalty if you qualify for a Special Enrollment Period.
- You will not pay a Part B penalty if you enroll in a Medicare Savings Program.
- Learn more about Special Enrollment Periods.
- You will pay an extra 10% for each year you could have signed up for Part B but did not.
- You may also pay a higher premium depending on your income.

Example:

If you waited 2 full years (24 months) to sign up for Part B and did not qualify for a Special Enrollment Period, you must pay a 20% late enrollment penalty. This is 10% for each full 12-month period that you could have signed up. You must also pay the standard Part B monthly premium ($202.90 in 2026).

+ $40.58 (20% of $202.90 late enrollment penalty)

$243.50 will be your Part B monthly premium for 2026. This amount ($243.48) is rounded to the nearest $.10 and includes the late enrollment penalty.

## Part D late enrollment penalty

- You usually do not pay a Part D penalty if:
  - You have creditable drug coverage (coverage that is similar in value to Part D) OR
  - You qualify for Extra Help

- You will pay an extra 1% for each month (that is 12% a year) if you:
  - Do not join a Medicare drug plan when you first get Medicare.
  - Go 63 days or more without creditable drug coverage.

- You may also pay a higher premium depending on your income.
- After you join a Medicare drug plan, the plan will tell you if you have to pay a penalty and what your premium will be.

- The national base beneficiary premium changes each year, so your penalty amount may also change each year. This monthly penalty is added for as long as you have Medicare drug coverage, even if you switch plans.

## Am I eligible?

To join a Medicare health plan or drug plan, you must have:

*   Medicare Part A and/or Part B.
*   One of these:
    *   Be a U.S. citizen or U.S. national.
    *   Be a lawful permanent resident (green card holder).
    *   Be a Cuban-Haitian entrant.
    *   Be lawfully living in the U.S. as a Compact of Free Association (COFA) migrant.
*   Live in the service area of the plan you want to join.
*   Have your Medicare Number.
*   Have your Part A and/or Part B coverage start dates. Find this on your Medicare card.

### When can I join?

You can only join, switch, or drop a Medicare Advantage Plan (Part C). You can also do this with or without drug coverage. You can only do this at certain times. These times are called enrollment periods.

## Initial Enrollment Period

Usually, this starts when you turn 65.

It lasts for 7 months. It starts 3 months before you turn 65. It ends 3 months after the month you turn 65. You might get Medicare earlier. This is if you have a disability, End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD), or ALS (also called Lou Gehrig’s disease). Learn more about when you can sign up in these situations.

You can join any plan. But you need this:

- Both Part A and Part B to join a Medicare Advantage Plan with or without drug coverage.
- Either Part A or Part B to join a Medicare drug plan.

- If you ask to join a plan after your Part A and/or Part B starts: Your plan coverage starts the first day of the month after the plan gets your request.

## Your first chance to sign up (Initial Enrollment Period)

This is your first chance to sign up. It happens when you turn 65. This time is called your Initial Enrollment Period. It lasts for 7 months. It starts 3 months before the month you turn 65. It ends 3 months after the month you turn 65.

### Avoid the penalty
If you miss your 7-month Initial Enrollment Period, you may have to wait to sign up. You may also have to pay a monthly late enrollment penalty. You pay this penalty for as long as you have Part B coverage. The penalty goes up the longer you wait. You may also have to pay a penalty if you have to pay a Part A premium. The date your coverage starts depends on which month you sign up during your Initial Enrollment Period. Coverage always starts on the first of the month.

## Joining a plan

After you sign up for Medicare, you can join a health or drug plan at some times.

To join a Medicare Advantage Plan (Part C):
*   You must have both Part A and Part B.

To join a Medicare drug plan (Part D):
*   You need only Part A or Part B.

Find out when you can join a plan.

Your total costs for Medicare drug coverage will depend on which plan you choose. Depending on the plan, you could pay:

- Premium: A monthly amount you pay for coverage, whether you get covered drugs or not.
  - Your specific premium will depend on the plan you choose. You may have to pay more, depending on your income.
  - Condition: Who pays a higher Part D premium because of income?
  - Condition: If you have to pay a Part D late enrollment penalty, it'll be added to your monthly premium.

Tip: Even if you don't take many drugs now, or your current out-of-pocket drug costs are low, consider getting a drug plan with a low monthly premium so you can avoid the late enrollment penalty. All plans must cover a wide range of drugs that people with Medicare take.

- Deductible: An amount you pay for covered drugs and items each year, before your plan starts to pay.
  - Your deductible will depend on which plan you choose.
  - Condition: No Medicare drug plan may have a deductible more than $700 in 2027 ($615 in 2026).
  - Condition: Some plans have no deductible.
- Copayment: A fixed amount you pay for a drug at the pharmacy.
- Coinsurance: A percentage you pay for a drug at the pharmacy.

### Medicare drug coverage stages

Generally, Medicare drug plans and Medicare Advantage Plans with drug coverage have 3 stages:

- Deductible stage: If your Medicare plan has a deductible, you pay all out-of-pocket costs until you reach the full deductible. No Medicare drug plan may have a deductible more than $615 in 2026 ($700 in 2027). Some Medicare drug plans don't have a deductible.
- Initial coverage stage: After you reach your full deductible (if your plan has a deductible), you pay 25% of the cost as coinsurance for your generic and brand-name drugs until your out-of-pocket spending on covered Part D drugs reaches $2,100 in 2026 ($2,400 in 2027)(including certain payments made on your behalf, like through the Extra Help program). Then, you get "catastrophic coverage" automatically.
- Catastrophic coverage stage: You won't pay out-of-pocket for covered Part D drugs for the rest of the calendar year.

When you have Medicare drug coverage, you get an Explanation of Benefits (EOB) the month after the pharmacy bills your plan. Your EOB shows the prescriptions you filled, what your plan paid, what you and others have paid, your coverage stage, and what counts toward your out-of-pocket costs and your total drug costs.

## How do I pay my plan’s premium?

You can choose to pay your premium by:

- Letting your plan take money from your checking or savings account.
- Using a credit or debit card (fees may apply).
- Getting a bill each month from your plan. Some plans bill in advance for next month’s coverage. Send your payment to the plan—not to Medicare. Ask your plan for their payment address.
- Having your plan take your premium from your Social Security payment. Contact your plan—not Social Security—to ask for this payment option. It may take up to 3 months to start.

If your plan did not take your premium from your Social Security payment for 1 or 2 months after you joined a Medicare drug plan, you will get a bill for those months. You will need to pay your drug plan’s monthly premium directly to your plan for those months. Your plan will tell you when your premium withholding from your Social Security payment is set up.

## How can I lower my drug costs?

If you qualify, programs can help lower your drug costs:

- Medicaid: This is a joint federal and state program. It helps cover medical costs for people with limited income and resources. Each state has different rules for income and resources to decide who qualifies. Contact your state to find out if you qualify.
- Extra Help: This is a Medicare program. It helps pay your drug costs. You automatically qualify for Extra Help if you qualify for Medicaid, one of the Medicare Savings Programs, or Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits from Social Security. If you do not automatically qualify for Extra Help, you can apply.

- Medicare's Limited Income Newly Eligible Transition (LI NET): This is a Medicare program. It gives temporary Medicare Part D drug coverage to people who qualify for Extra Help or Medicaid but who are not yet enrolled in a Medicare drug plan. LI NET covers all Part D covered drugs. There are no network pharmacy restrictions.

- State Pharmaceutical Assistance Programs (SPAP): These programs provide coverage from your state (or the U.S. Virgin Islands). They help pay your drug plan premiums and/or cost sharing. SPAP contributions may count toward your Medicare drug coverage out-of-pocket limit. Eligibility depends on each program's specific rules.
- Pharmaceutical Assistance Programs (sometimes called Patient Assistance Programs (PAPs)): Some pharmaceutical companies offer programs. They help pay for medications for people enrolled in Medicare drug coverage (Part D). Find out if there is a Pharmaceutical Assistance Program (PAP) that can lower prescription costs for the drugs you take. Each company has different eligibility requirements to join their program. Contact the company to find out if you qualify and start getting help.

The Medicare Prescription Payment Plan is a new payment option. It works with your current Medicare drug coverage. It helps you manage your out-of-pocket costs for drugs covered by your plan. It does this by spreading costs across the calendar year (January–December). This payment option might help you manage your monthly expenses. It does not save you money or lower your drug costs.

## What is the Part D late enrollment penalty?

The Part D late enrollment penalty is a fee. This fee is added to your Medicare drug coverage (Part D) premium. This fee stays with you forever. You may have to pay this fee if there are 63 or more days in a row after your Initial Enrollment Period ends. This happens if you do not have Medicare drug coverage or other creditable prescription drug coverage during those days. When you join a Medicare drug plan, the plan will tell you two things: if you must pay the penalty and what your premium will be. You must pay this penalty for as long as you have Medicare drug coverage.

### How much is the Part D late enrollment penalty?

The Part D late enrollment penalty is calculated by multiplying 1% times the "national base beneficiary premium" ($38.99 in 2026) times the number of full, uncovered months you were eligible to join Medicare drug coverage but did not (and did not have other creditable prescription drug coverage).

That amount is rounded to the nearest $.10. This rounded amount is added to your monthly premium. The "national base beneficiary premium" may go up each year. So your penalty amount may go up each year.

Example: If you waited 14 months after you were eligible for Medicare to join a Medicare drug plan, and you did not have creditable drug coverage, you will have to pay a 14% late enrollment penalty. You must pay this on top of your monthly plan premium. Here is the math for the monthly Part D enrollment penalty.

The Part D late enrollment penalty is added to your premium for as long as you have Medicare drug coverage. This is true even if you switch plans. However, if you get Extra Help, you do not pay a late enrollment penalty.

## If a hospital changes your status from "inpatient" to "outpatient with observation services"

A court order gave you the right to appeal. You can appeal if a hospital changes your status from "inpatient" to "outpatient." This only applies if you also meet certain other rules.

You can ask for an appeal if:
*   You were admitted to the hospital as an inpatient on or after January 1, 2009.
*   The hospital changed your status to "outpatient getting observation services."
*   You meet certain other rules.

You can ask for a fast appeal while you are still in the hospital if:
*   You were admitted to the hospital as an inpatient.
*   The hospital changed your status to "outpatient getting observation services."

### Why does hospital status matter?

Your hospital status changes how much you pay for hospital services. Your hospital status may also change if Medicare covers care in a skilled nursing facility (SNF) after your hospital stay.
